## 1. Breakdown of the 6 Side Symbols

Flanking George Eastman’s central portrait profile are **six small square bronze panels** (three on the left, three on the right). Designed in an Art Deco, low-relief style, each symbol represents a foundational pillar of Eastman’s life, industry, and philosophy.

```
       LEFT SIDE                 RIGHT SIDE
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Top-Left:           |   | Top-Right:          |
| Light Rays & Prism  |   | Woven Film Web      |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Middle-Left:        |   | Middle-Right:       |
| Chemical Retort     |   | Torches of Learning |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Bottom-Left:        |   | Bottom-Right:       |
| Mechanical Gears    |   | Globe & Meridian    |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+

```

### Top-Left: Light Rays through a Prism (Optics & Physics)

* **Visual:** Stylized linear rays of light passing through a refraction angle / lens geometry.
* **Meaning:** Represents the physics of light and optics, the fundamental scientific basis of photography. It reflects Eastman’s obsession with capturing light accurately through precision lenses and exposure control.

### Middle-Left: Chemical Retort & Flask (Applied Chemistry)

* **Visual:** A classic glass chemical retort/flask resting over heat or set against laboratory lines.
* **Meaning:** Represents chemistry and emulsion technology. Eastman’s greatest breakthrough was transforming heavy, messy wet-plate photography into dry gelatin plates and flexible roll film through continuous chemical experimentation.

before.text: Everything else follows. Motion pictures ran on his film, and he arranged the industry so they could run on no one else's. He gave away most of a fortune while he was alive rather than leaving a foundation behind him, and he gave much of it anonymously, including a gift to MIT large enough to fund the institute's move across the Charles at the moment Harvard was maneuvering to absorb it. He delivered it under a false name and kept the secret for eight years. In 1912 he bought a company in London in order to acquire one scientist, and told him his job was the future of photography. That laboratory produced Kodachrome, and color is what turned a photograph from a record into a memory.

notes.chunk_at_written: Twenty-five years later, on the evening of March 5, 1912, he sat down at the Hotel Belmont in New York with the president of MIT. The institute was financially strapped and Harvard was maneuvering to absorb it, and the two men talked into the night about a new campus across the Charles. Eastman asked what sum would be needed. Two and a half million, Maclaurin said. Eastman said he would send a draft for that amount. His only condition was that nobody know who had sent it. May I tell my wife, Maclaurin asked. Well, yes, Eastman said, but no one else. The secret held for eight years, and he asked for nothing in return: no name on any building, no publicity, no say in anything.
